'''''World of Echo''''' is the second studio album by American musician [[Arthur Russell (musician)|Arthur Russell]], released in 1986 on [[Upside Records]] in the US and in 1987 on [[Rough Trade Records]] in the UK. It is composed primarily of Russell's vocals, cello, and percussion, which are liberally treated with [[audio signal processing|effects]] such as [[delay (audio effect)|delay]] and [[reverb]].

''World of Echo'' was the final album released by Russell during his lifetime. It was widely reissued in 2005 by Audika and Rough Trade. The album was named the best of the 1980s by ''[[Fact (UK magazine)|Fact]]'' in 2013,<ref name="FACT Magazine review">{{Cite news |last=Lea |first=Tom |date=2013-06-24 |title=The 100 Best Albums Of The 1980s |url=https://www.factmag.com/2013/06/24/the-100-best-albums-of-the-1980s-100-81/101/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403233552/https://www.factmag.com/2013/06/24/the-100-best-albums-of-the-1980s-100-81/101/ |archive-date=2023-04-03 |access-date=2025-08-31 |work=Fact Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> and the 25th best album of the decade by ''[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]'' in 2018.<ref name="Pelly">{{cite web |last=Pelly |first=Jenn |title=The 200 Best Albums of the 1980s |url=https://pitchfork.com/features/lists-and-guides/the-200-best-albums-of-the-1980s/?page=9 |website=Pitchfork |access-date=9 December 2022}}</ref> It was included in ''[[New Musical Express|NME]]''{{'}}s 2013 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time.<ref name="nme.com">{{cite magazine |title=The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time |url=https://www.nme.com/photos/the-500-greatest-albums-of-all-time-400-301-1426436 |magazine=NME |date=October 23, 2013}}</ref>

==Background and composition==
''World of Echo'' has been noted as prominently incorporating Russell's "folksy [[tenor]], [[cello]], and scant electronic [[microtone]]s".<ref name="pitchfork" /> It features Russell's employment of [[Music production|production effects]], including prominent use of [[Delay (audio effect)|echo]], [[reverb]], and [[Distortion (music)|distortion]].<ref name="pitchfork" /> [[AllMusic]] referred to the album as a collection of "spare, dubby cello experiments."<ref name="allbio">{{cite web|url = https://www.allmusic.com/artist/arthur-russell-mn0000475362 | title = Arthur Russell | access-date = October 29, 2007 | first = Richard | last = Pierson | work = [[Allmusic]] }}</ref> Several songs included are alternate versions of dance tracks that Russell produced as [[12-inch single]]s, including "Let's Go Swimming", "Wax the Van", and "Treehouse".<ref name="allmusic">{{cite web|url = https://www.allmusic.com/artist/arthur-russell-mn0000475362 | title = Arthur Russell | access-date = October 29, 2007 | author = Richard Pierson | work = [[Allmusic]] }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Leland |first=John |date=December 1986 |title=Singles - review |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FL-rqqrDxb8C&pg=PA46 |journal=[[Spin (magazine)|SPIN]] |volume=2 |issue=9 |pages=47 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

Writing for [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']], Cameron Macdonald noted that Russell's style of cello playing, often improvised, makes use of sporadic, imaginary sounds like "hollow thuds, window-washing brushes, chipped strings, knuckled knacks, and the boom of a floor peg dropping on concrete".<ref name="pitchfork" /> He also commented that the cello "startlingly duets with his voice", leading to [[Inharmonicity|inharmonic]] sounds that makes it sound like the instrument "clears its throat during his awkward moments".<ref name="pitchfork" /> ''Dusted'' also commented on the album's "skeletal framework", with "bare melodies rising to the surface, vocal lines encompassing wordless singing" and "constantly shifting textures swirling throughout".<ref name="dusted">{{cite web|url=http://www.dustedmagazine.com/reviews/1829|title=Dusted Reviews: Arthur Russell - World of Echo|work=Dusted Magazine|date=November 14, 2004|accessdate=April 1, 2019}}</ref>

==Release==
The album was released in the US in 1986 and subsequently in the UK in March 1987.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Record News |magazine=[[NME]] |date=March 28, 1987 |page=33}}</ref> When it failed to perform well commercially, Russell reportedly requested that stickers be added to the packaging with the word "unintelligible."<ref name="Pelly"/>

Audika Records issued a remastered limited edition CD in 2004 which included bonus tracks and a DVD with footage by [[Phill Niblock]]. They subsequently reissued it on CD and LP in 2005. Rough Trade also reissued the album that year.

===Early reviews===
In a 1987 review for ''[[Melody Maker]]'', [[David Stubbs]] positively described the music as "a fuzz, a blur, a rich, throbbing pulse, a signal in space", and Russell's vocals as "clotted, opaque, word-shapes in the clouds", noting a kinship with [[John Martyn]]'s 1973 album ''[[Solid Air]]''. He called the result "a giant, subterranean repository of [[Dub music|Dub]]", and said, "what's at work is the old dub trick of suggesting what's not there, what's been dispensed with".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Stubbs |first=David |author-link=David Stubbs |title=Arthur Russell - ''World of Echo'' |magazine=[[Melody Maker]] |date=April 11, 1987 |page=33}}</ref> Jonathan Romney of ''[[NME]]'' stated that "''World of Echo'' contains some of Russell's golden greats, but the catch is that they're virtually unrecognisable", and also made a comparison to John Martyn "at his spaciest". Romney concluded that "it's fun watching the patterns change, but you sometimes get tired waiting for something to happen".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Romney |first=Jonathan |title=Arthur Russell – ''World of Echo'' |magazine=[[NME]] |date=April 4, 1987 |page=32}}</ref> More negatively, a ''[[Q (magazine)|Q]]'' review by Andy Gill said, "On this LP, unfortunately, the imagination displayed on the three mixes of [previous dance single] 'Let's Go Swimming' is all but completely absent", and that the titles of the songs "betray Arthur as just another art bore caught on the less meaningful fringes of [[New-age music|New Age]] [[muzak]]. A big disappointment."<ref name="Q">{{cite magazine |last=Gill |first=Andy |title=Arthur Russell – ''World of Echo'' |magazine=[[Q (magazine)|Q]] |issue=8 |date=May 1987 |page=78}}</ref>

===Later reception and accolades===
Reviewing the album's 2004 reissue, ''Dusted'' called the album "easily the most significant, compelling, beautiful and monumental piece of work Russell ever committed to record."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Crumsho |first1=Michael |title=Dusted Reviews: Arthur Russell - World of Echo |url=http://www.dustedmagazine.com/reviews/1829 |website=Dusted |access-date=27 December 2024}}</ref> ''[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]'' stated that "this material still sounds timeless. It's also Russell's most personal and radical statement."<ref name="pitchfork"/> ''[[AllMusic]]'' described the album as an "incredible assemblage of ... subtle, transcendental" music.<ref name="Tyranny" /> ''[[Stylus Magazine]]'' opined that the album "still appears fantastic, implausible, and above all, fresh," claiming that "Russell's tapestries of [[Electroacoustic music|electro-acoustic]] syncopation and [[Free association (psychology)|free-associative]] song can still be heard" in styles such as [[intelligent dance music|IDM]], [[minimal techno]], modern [[psychedelic music|psychedelia]], and freeform acoustic music.<ref name="Stylus" /> In a 2024 article for the ''[[London Review of Books]]'', [[Ian Penman]] described the music as "sitting-room [[dub music]], folk song with [[Tape delay (audio effect)|tape delay]] [...] a musical [[Impressionism]] where background and foreground merge in a dappled, smeary haze. These songs don’t feel ‘written’ in any conventional way; they are like pollen on the breeze."<ref name="lrb">{{cite web |last1=Penman |first1=Ian |title=Nom de Boom: Arthur Russell's Benediction |url=https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v46/n16/ian-penman/nom-de-boom |website=[[London Review of Books]] |access-date=27 December 2024}}</ref>

In 2013, the album was ranked at number 301 on ''NME''{{'}}s list of the 500 greatest albums of all time.<ref name="nme.com"/> in the same year, it was also named the best album of the 1980s by ''[[Fact (UK magazine)|Fact]]''.<ref name="FACT Magazine review"/> In 2018, it was ranked the 25th best album of the 1980s by ''[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]''.<ref name="Pelly"/>

==In popular culture==
In 2016, American rapper and producer [[Kanye West]] sampled a section from Russell's "Answers Me" in his song "[[30 Hours]]".<ref>{{Cite web|title = Kanye West Shares New Song "30 Hours," Adds More Songs to New Album The Life of Pablo|url = http://pitchfork.com/news/63499-kanye-west-shares-new-song-30-hours-adds-more-songs-to-new-album-the-life-of-pablo/|website = Pitchfork| date=12 February 2016 |access-date = 2016-02-12|language = en-US}}</ref>
